title: The prophet Harris
hook: a Liberian evangelist walks West Africa in a white robe, and tradition says crowds are baptized

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sadhu Sundar Singh and his railway story: the gospel's water in an Indian cup.

A prison cell in Liberia. The man inside is a schoolteacher and church worker named William Wadé Harris, locked up for his part in a political protest. By his own account, an angel comes to him there in a vision and tells him to put away his European clothes, dress simply, and go out as a preacher. When he walks out of prison, he does exactly that: a long white gown, a tall staff with a cross on top, a Bible, and a gourd rattle to call people together. No mission board sent him. No salary is waiting. He sets off along the coast on foot.
screen: `A WHITE GOWN, A CROSS-STAFF, A BIBLE.`

segments.voice: Harris walked east, out of Liberia, along the coast of what is now Côte d'Ivoire and into what is now Ghana. Village to village, on foot. He preached in simple words, prayed for the sick, and baptized people who wanted to follow Jesus. Tradition says the crowds grew so large that colonial officials grew nervous and finally sent him back home. His time on the road was short. Then the surprise. Harris didn't build his own organization. He told the new believers to build simple prayer houses, keep Sunday, and wait: teachers with the Bible would come, and they should listen. Then he walked on. Years later, missionaries arriving in some of those villages found congregations already gathered, keeping Sunday, singing, and waiting for someone to teach them. Some joined the Methodist church. Others kept his name and founded the Harrist Church, which continues today. Christians describe him differently: an evangelist, a prophet, a forerunner of the independent African churches. He called himself a prophet. Isaiah has a line for people like him, in the King James Bible: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace." It praises the feet. Not the voice, not the robe. Harris preached with his walking. Every village heard him because he had walked there.

If you can, stand and walk slowly, in a room or outside, feeling each step land, heel then toe; if you can't walk, let each breath be a step. With each step, name one person or place you'll pass today: the office, the bus driver, a neighbor's door. If you pray, carry each one to God as you go; if not, simply carry them with you.
Harris. A Liberian preacher who walked the West African coast in a white gown with a cross-staff, telling new believers to wait for teachers with the Bible.
Your line: the walking prophet. He let his feet do the preaching. Day nine hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Members of the Harrist Church in Côte d'Ivoire, and some Methodists in the region, remember William Wadé Harris as the preacher who first brought the gospel to their villages.
